title: Prompt elements are requirement types
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:00 (optional self-study; no live allocation)

PURPOSE: Support independent study with the detailed explanation or checked exercise material.

LAND THIS: A prompt specifies the content, behavior, and quality of a reply or artifact.

SAY:
- This page provides prompt elements are requirement types.
- Use it independently after the workshop and check important statements against the source.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Optional self-study. Return to the related live slide or continue the reference material as needed.

IF LATE: SKIP

REQUIREMENT TYPE MENU
Functional behavior: What the artifact must do: filter, calculate, extract, compare, or explain.
Acceptance evidence: Exercise each requested behavior.

Data and provenance: Allowed inputs, definitions, period, revision, and traceability.
Acceptance evidence: Trace a result to the right source record.

Scope and exclusions: What is included, excluded, or explicitly outside the task.
Acceptance evidence: Check boundary cases and excluded records.

Audience and use: Who will use the result and the decision or action it supports.
Acceptance evidence: Have a representative reader use the output.

Role and working behavior: A perspective plus observable conduct; a title alone is weak guidance.
Acceptance evidence: Check the requested conduct, such as stating assumptions.

Content and completeness: Required topics, facts, fields, decisions, and limitations.
Acceptance evidence: Compare output against a coverage checklist.

Method and business rules: Formulas, grouping rules, denominators, precedence, and missing-data treatment.
Acceptance evidence: Independently recompute or trace a worked example.

Structure and interface: Sections, tabs, slides, columns, controls, and navigation.
Acceptance evidence: Inspect structure and exercise navigation.

Tone and presentation: Voice, reading level, units, number formats, and visual emphasis.
Acceptance evidence: Use a concrete rubric and a representative example.

Accessibility and usability: Readable contrast, meaningful labels, keyboard access, and understandable language.
Acceptance evidence: Try the relevant reading or interaction tasks.

Quality and acceptance: Observable correctness, completeness, reliability, and performance criteria.
Acceptance evidence: Define the test input and expected result.

Constraints and authority: Allowed tools, dependencies, data access, edits, approvals, and stop conditions.
Acceptance evidence: Inspect actions and configured permissions where applicable.

Delivery and compatibility: File type, editability, offline use, destination, and supported application.
Acceptance evidence: Open the delivered file in the intended environment.

Maintenance and reuse: Refresh procedure, source version, change notes, and reusable parameters.
Acceptance evidence: Repeat the task with changed input and compare behavior.

This artifact taxonomy is an instructional application, not a formal standard. Context may contain facts as well as constraints. Use only the relevant, consistent, feasible requirements. See slide 90 for requirements-writing sources.

title: Spreadsheet analysis: requirements to choose
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:00 (optional self-study; no live allocation)

PURPOSE: Support independent study with the detailed explanation or checked exercise material.

LAND THIS: Data requirements define which records and calculations are valid.

SAY:
- This page provides spreadsheet analysis: requirements to choose.
- Use it independently after the workshop and check important statements against the source.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Optional self-study. Return to the related live slide or continue the reference material as needed.

IF LATE: SKIP

REQUIREMENT TYPE MENU
Row grain: State that each detail row is a month–site–supplier observation.
Acceptance evidence: Confirm grouping keys before aggregation.

Reporting period: Use an explicit inclusive month range from Month.
Acceptance evidence: Check the first and last included months.

Field types and units: Treat Month as a month; identify counts, percentages, hours, and currency.
Acceptance evidence: Check parsing and unit labels.

Duplicates and summary rows: Exclude the existing TOTAL row and investigate duplicate keys.
Acceptance evidence: Compare row counts and a duplicate-key report.

Metric definition: Define return rate as sum of Units_Returned divided by sum of Units_Shipped.
Acceptance evidence: Recompute the numerator, denominator, and displayed rate.

Weighting and denominators: Do not infer overall on-time delivery from monthly percentages without delivery counts.
Acceptance evidence: Flag the missing denominator instead of claiming an overall rate.

Missing and invalid values: Retain the missing Inspection_Hours value; disclose any exclusion.
Acceptance evidence: Inspect missing-value counts and affected calculations.

Segmentation and comparison: Compare suppliers on the same selected period and sites.
Acceptance evidence: Confirm equal filter scope for each comparison.

Rounding and number formats: Display return rates to three decimal places while retaining calculation precision.
Acceptance evidence: Check displayed 0.348% against the underlying ratio.

Formula traceability: Use inspectable formulas or an included calculation log.
Acceptance evidence: Trace one output to its input rows.

Structure and usability: Provide a scorecard tab and a definitions tab with meaningful headers.
Acceptance evidence: Open both tabs and identify the measure without outside explanation.

Verification and limitations: Reconcile counts and sums; distinguish association from a causal explanation.
Acceptance evidence: Compare totals and challenge unsupported explanations.

Delivery and portability: Deliver an editable Excel workbook (.xlsx) with no broken external references.
Acceptance evidence: Open the file in the intended spreadsheet application.

This artifact taxonomy is an instructional application, not a formal standard. Context may contain facts as well as constraints. Use only the relevant, consistent, feasible requirements. See slide 90 for requirements-writing sources.

title: HTML dashboards: requirements to choose
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:00 (optional self-study; no live allocation)

PURPOSE: Support independent study with the detailed explanation or checked exercise material.

LAND THIS: An interactive dashboard needs behavior and state requirements as well as visual requirements.

SAY:
- This page provides html dashboards: requirements to choose.
- Use it independently after the workshop and check important statements against the source.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Optional self-study. Return to the related live slide or continue the reference material as needed.

IF LATE: SKIP

REQUIREMENT TYPE MENU
Input contract: Embed the checked supplier detail data and identify the snapshot date.
Acceptance evidence: Compare record count and source identifiers.

Date range: Use month selectors matching the source granularity; include both endpoints.
Acceptance evidence: Test a single month and the full range.

Category controls: Offer Supplier and Site multi-select controls; Type or Class requires a real source field.
Acceptance evidence: Compare each option with actual distinct values.

Grouping and granularity: Allow grouping by supplier, site, or month when relevant to the decision.
Acceptance evidence: Check counts and totals after changing the grouping.

Metric selection: Offer named measures with definitions and units.
Acceptance evidence: Verify that labels, scales, and calculations all change together.

Filter combination: Apply selected filters consistently, with an explicit AND/OR rule.
Acceptance evidence: Use a known intersection and compare included records.

Coordinated views: Charts, totals, and tables must represent the same selected records.
Acceptance evidence: Reconcile a chart total with its underlying table.

Sorting and drill-down: Sort numerically and allow inspection of supporting rows.
Acceptance evidence: Compare sorted order and inspect a selected group.

Empty, missing, and zero states: Distinguish no matching records from a valid zero; avoid division by zero.
Acceptance evidence: Exercise all three cases.

Reset and visible state: Show active selections and restore the default state with Reset.
Acceptance evidence: Change multiple controls, reset, and compare the initial view.

Accessibility and layout: Use labeled controls, visible focus, readable contrast, and a usable narrow layout.
Acceptance evidence: Navigate by keyboard and test a smaller window.

Portability and dependencies: Deliver one self-contained HyperText Markup Language (.html) file with embedded data and no required network calls.
Acceptance evidence: Open offline and inspect for missing assets.

Performance: Choose a measurable response target on the training laptop for this dataset.
Acceptance evidence: Time a representative filter change; do not invent a universal target.

Export and reconciliation: If export is needed, export the filtered data and retain the chosen scope.
Acceptance evidence: Compare exported rows with the displayed selection.

This artifact taxonomy is an instructional application, not a formal standard. Context may contain facts as well as constraints. Use only the relevant, consistent, feasible requirements. See slide 90 for requirements-writing sources.

title: Presentations: requirements to choose
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:00 (optional self-study; no live allocation)

PURPOSE: Support independent study with the detailed explanation or checked exercise material.

LAND THIS: A presentation needs audience, narrative, visual, and delivery requirements.

SAY:
- This page provides presentations: requirements to choose.
- Use it independently after the workshop and check important statements against the source.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Optional self-study. Return to the related live slide or continue the reference material as needed.

IF LATE: SKIP

REQUIREMENT TYPE MENU
Purpose and audience: Name the decision, audience knowledge, and intended action.
Acceptance evidence: A reviewer can identify the decision and next step.

Scope and slide count: For the mock presentation, request five slides with a defined coverage list.
Acceptance evidence: Count slides and map each required topic.

Story structure: Move from business question to evidence, implications, and next action.
Acceptance evidence: Read only the titles and check the narrative.

Message hierarchy: Use one main message per slide; make evidence support that message.
Acceptance evidence: Ask a reader what to remember first.

Data fidelity: Use only checked findings and preserve period, units, and limitations.
Acceptance evidence: Reconcile displayed values with the workbook.

Chart semantics: Choose an appropriate chart, truthful axes, and clearly labeled categories.
Acceptance evidence: Check that the encoding supports the claimed comparison.

Typography and readability: Set readable projected text and avoid dense paragraphs on teaching slides.
Acceptance evidence: Inspect at presentation size and the expected viewing distance.

Visual consistency: Use a restrained palette, aligned margins, and consistent emphasis.
Acceptance evidence: Compare consecutive slides as a set.

Speaker notes: Provide purpose, talking points, transitions, and exercise instructions.
Acceptance evidence: Inspect notes on every relevant slide.

Timing and mode: Classify TEACH, DO, REFERENCE, and DIVIDER; protect 30 practice minutes.
Acceptance evidence: Sum notes and rehearse the live path.

Reference completeness: Make self-study slides understandable without the facilitator.
Acceptance evidence: Have a reader explain the example from the slide and notes.

Accessibility: Use readable contrast and descriptive alternatives for meaningful visuals.
Acceptance evidence: Review with the target presentation application’s accessibility tools.

Delivery and editability: Deliver an editable PowerPoint (.pptx), retaining notes and usable charts.
Acceptance evidence: Open, edit, and present the exported file.

title: Email summaries: requirements to choose
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:00 (optional self-study; no live allocation)

PURPOSE: Support independent study with the detailed explanation or checked exercise material.

LAND THIS: A useful summary preserves evidence, chronology, ownership, and conditions.

SAY:
- This page provides email summaries: requirements to choose.
- Use it independently after the workshop and check important statements against the source.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Optional self-study. Return to the related live slide or continue the reference material as needed.

IF LATE: SKIP

REQUIREMENT TYPE MENU
Source scope: Name the selected thread, relevant date range, and available attachments.
Acceptance evidence: List the messages and attachments actually used.

Current state: Separate the latest position from earlier proposals.
Acceptance evidence: Trace each changed date to the message that superseded it.

Decision extraction: Distinguish approved, proposed, rejected, and unresolved items.
Acceptance evidence: Compare decision status with the source wording.

Conditional approval: Keep the cost cap and quality sign-off attached to the approval.
Acceptance evidence: Reject a summary that says simply approved.

Actions and ownership: Extract action, explicit owner, due date, and status.
Acceptance evidence: Check each field; use Not stated for missing details.

Date meaning: Distinguish a trial date, change date, and action due date.
Acceptance evidence: Check that September 25 and October 2 are not conflated.

Open questions and conflicts: List unresolved freight responsibility and contradictory statements.
Acceptance evidence: Locate the source question and any subsequent resolution.

Evidence traceability: Use message dates, senders, and supporting excerpts or available links.
Acceptance evidence: Open the referenced message and verify the claim.

Attachments and missing input: Flag a mentioned drawing that is not available to the assistant.
Acceptance evidence: Do not summarize content of an unavailable attachment.

Format and tone: Provide a neutral current-state brief and a separate action table.
Acceptance evidence: Check that opinions are labeled and actions are easy to scan.

Access and tool availability: Use only mail and attachments available in the actual Copilot and Outlook setup.
Acceptance evidence: Confirm retrieval scope; use the supplied-text exercise when needed.

Authority and delivery: Prepare any reply as a draft for human review; do not send automatically.
Acceptance evidence: Inspect the draft and action record.

title: Plain-language documents: requirements to choose
notes:
MODE: REFERENCE

TIME: 0:00 (optional self-study; no live allocation)

PURPOSE: Support independent study with the detailed explanation or checked exercise material.

LAND THIS: Accessible language must preserve meaning, conditions, and useful detail.

SAY:
- This page provides plain-language documents: requirements to choose.
- Use it independently after the workshop and check important statements against the source.

DO: None.

BRIDGE: Optional self-study. Return to the related live slide or continue the reference material as needed.

IF LATE: SKIP

REQUIREMENT TYPE MENU
Reader and purpose: Write for a reader at a fifth-grade reading level who needs to understand or do a named task.
Acceptance evidence: A representative reader can state the purpose.

Source and factual scope: Use the supplied source and identify unsupported or missing information.
Acceptance evidence: Trace factual claims to the source.

Concept coverage: List the ideas the reader must understand before drafting.
Acceptance evidence: Compare the document with the coverage list.

Vocabulary: Prefer familiar words and define necessary technical terms at first use.
Acceptance evidence: Review unfamiliar terms and their definitions.

Sentence and paragraph structure: Use short direct sentences and one main idea per paragraph.
Acceptance evidence: Read aloud and inspect complex sentences.

Organization: Use meaningful headings and ordered steps when order matters.
Acceptance evidence: Ask a reader to locate the first action and a key explanation.

Examples and analogies: Include a concrete everyday example and state the limit of any analogy.
Acceptance evidence: Check that the analogy does not change the underlying idea.

Tone and respect: Use a clear adult tone without condescension or childish phrasing.
Acceptance evidence: Review wording with the intended audience.

Accuracy and caveats: Preserve important conditions, uncertainty, exceptions, and warnings from the source.
Acceptance evidence: Compare the simplified version with the original meaning.

Readability evidence: Use reading-level estimates as one signal, plus human comprehension checks.
Acceptance evidence: Do not claim exact grade-level comprehension from a score alone.

Visual support and accessibility: Use a labeled diagram or example only when it improves understanding.
Acceptance evidence: Ask what the visual helps the reader explain.

Comprehension check: Provide three questions and a short answer key grounded in the document.
Acceptance evidence: Confirm the answers can be found or inferred from the text.

Delivery and reuse: Specify an editable document, useful headings, and reusable topic placeholders.
Acceptance evidence: Open the output and adapt one topic without losing the structure.

This artifact taxonomy is an instructional application, not a formal standard. Context may contain facts as well as constraints. Use only the relevant, consistent, feasible requirements. See slide 90 for requirements-writing sources.
